# Direction Angle of a 2D Vector in Terms of Arctangent

## Statement

Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in a Cartesian plane $P$, expressed in component form with respect to the standard basis $\left(\mathbf i,\mathbf j\right)$ as
$$\mathbf a = x\,\mathbf i + y\,\mathbf j .$$
Let $\theta$ denote the direction of $\mathbf a$, measured from the positive direction of the $x$-axis, and taken in the half-open interval $\hointl{-\pi}{\pi} = (-\pi,\pi]$.

Then
$$\theta = \begin{cases}
\arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) & x > 0\\[2pt]
\arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) + \pi & x < 0,\ y \ge 0\\[2pt]
\arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) - \pi & x < 0,\ y < 0\\[2pt]
\dfrac\pi2 & x = 0,\ y > 0\\[2pt]
-\dfrac\pi2 & x = 0,\ y < 0\\[2pt]
\text{undefined} & x = 0,\ y = 0 ,
\end{cases}$$
where $\arctan$ is the real arctangent function, with values in $\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$.

---

## Part I. Conventions, and the analytic form of the hypothesis

### I.1 Magnitude

Write
$$r := \left\lvert\mathbf a\right\rvert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}.$$
Then $r \ge 0$, and $r = 0$ if and only if $x = y = 0$, i.e. if and only if $\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$.

### I.2 The direction of a vector, and its analytic characterisation

The *direction* of a nonzero vector quantity $\mathbf a$ in the plane is the angle through which the positive $x$-axis must be rotated about the origin in order to bring it into coincidence with the ray from the origin along $\mathbf a$; by the usual convention this angle is reckoned **positive anticlockwise** and **negative clockwise**, and is normalised to lie in $(-\pi,\pi]$.

We first put this in analytic form.

**Lemma 0.** Let $\mathbf a = x\mathbf i + y\mathbf j \ne \mathbf 0$, and let $r = \left\lvert\mathbf a\right\rvert > 0$. An angle $\theta$ is a direction of $\mathbf a$ in the above sense if and only if
$$\cos\theta = \frac xr \quad\text{and}\quad \sin\theta = \frac yr, \tag{$\ast$}$$
equivalently, if and only if
$$\mathbf a = r\left(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j\right). \tag{$\ast\ast$}$$

*Proof.* Identify $P$ with $\R^2$ via the standard basis, so that $\mathbf a$ is the position vector of the point $A = (x,y)$ and $\mathbf i$ is the position vector of $I = (1,0)$, the point where the positive $x$-axis meets the unit circle $S = \left\{(u,v) : u^2+v^2 = 1\right\}$.

Since $r>0$, the vector $\mathbf u := \dfrac1r\mathbf a = \dfrac xr\mathbf i + \dfrac yr\mathbf j$ is a positive scalar multiple of $\mathbf a$, so it points along the same ray from the origin as $\mathbf a$; and
$$\left(\frac xr\right)^2 + \left(\frac yr\right)^2 = \frac{x^2+y^2}{r^2} = 1,$$
so the endpoint $U := \left(\dfrac xr, \dfrac yr\right)$ of $\mathbf u$ lies on $S$.

Moreover $U$ is the **only** point of $S$ on that ray. Indeed, the ray from the origin along $\mathbf a$ consists exactly of the points with position vector $t\,\mathbf u$ for $t \ge 0$, and for such $t$,
$$\left\lvert t\,\mathbf u\right\rvert = t\left\lvert\mathbf u\right\rvert = t,$$
which equals $1$ if and only if $t=1$. So the ray meets $S$ in the single point $U$.

Hence rotating the positive $x$-axis about the origin onto the ray along $\mathbf a$ is the same thing as rotating the point $I$ (which lies on $S$, and which every rotation about the origin keeps on $S$) onto the point $U$: a rotation maps the positive $x$-axis onto the ray precisely when it maps $I$ into the ray, and the only point of $S$ available as the image is $U$.

Now, by the very definition of the circular functions, for any real $\theta$ the rotation about the origin through the angle $\theta$ (anticlockwise for $\theta>0$, clockwise for $\theta<0$) carries $I = (1,0)$ to the point $\left(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right)$ of $S$. Hence the rotation through $\theta$ carries the positive $x$-axis onto the ray along $\mathbf a$ if and only if
$$\left(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right) = U = \left(\frac xr,\frac yr\right),$$
which is exactly $(\ast)$. Finally, $(\ast)$ and $(\ast\ast)$ are equivalent: multiplying $(\ast)$ by $r$ and using that $\left(\mathbf i,\mathbf j\right)$ is a basis (so that two vectors are equal precisely when their components agree) gives $(\ast\ast)$, and conversely. $\blacksquare$

So, for $\mathbf a \ne \mathbf 0$, the theorem to be proved is the assertion that the unique $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi]$ satisfying $(\ast)$ is the one given by the case formula. Uniqueness is Lemma 1 below; existence will come out of the construction.

### I.3 The zero vector

If $x = y = 0$ then $r = 0$ and $\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$. The zero vector determines no ray from the origin — every point of the plane, and in particular every point of the unit circle, is "in its direction" only vacuously; formally, $(\ast\ast)$ reads $\mathbf 0 = 0\cdot(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j)$, which holds for **every** $\theta$, so no angle is singled out. Accordingly the direction of $\mathbf 0$ is undefined, which is the last line of the case formula. (Note that $(\ast)$ itself is not even formable, since it involves division by $r=0$.)

### I.4 Properties of $\arctan$

$\arctan : \R \to \openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ is the inverse of the restriction of $\tan$ to $\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$, on which $\tan$ is a strictly increasing bijection onto $\R$. Hence for all $u \in \R$:
$$\arctan u \in \left(-\tfrac\pi2,\ \tfrac\pi2\right), \qquad \tan\left(\arctan u\right) = u. \tag{A1}$$
Being the inverse of a strictly increasing function, $\arctan$ is itself strictly increasing; and $\arctan 0 = 0$ because $\tan 0 = 0$ with $0 \in \openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$. Consequently
$$u > 0 \implies \arctan u \in \left(0,\tfrac\pi2\right), \qquad
u = 0 \implies \arctan u = 0, \qquad
u < 0 \implies \arctan u \in \left(-\tfrac\pi2,\ 0\right). \tag{A2}$$

### I.5 Trigonometric facts used

For $\phi \in \openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ we have $\cos\phi > 0$; and wherever $\cos\phi \ne 0$,
$$\tan\phi = \frac{\sin\phi}{\cos\phi}, \qquad 1 + \tan^2\phi = \sec^2\phi = \frac1{\cos^2\phi}. \tag{T1}$$
For all real $\psi$,
$$\cos(\psi\pm\pi) = -\cos\psi, \qquad \sin(\psi\pm\pi) = -\sin\psi, \tag{T2}$$
$$\cos\psi = 1 \iff \psi \in 2\pi\Z, \tag{T3}$$
and the subtraction formula $\cos(\alpha-\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta$, together with $\cos^2\alpha+\sin^2\alpha = 1$.

---

## Part II. Two lemmas

### Lemma 1 (uniqueness of the normalised angle)

**Lemma 1.** Let $c,s \in \R$. There is at most one $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta = c$ and $\sin\theta = s$.

*Proof.* Suppose $\theta_1,\theta_2 \in (-\pi,\pi]$ both satisfy these two equations. By the cosine subtraction formula,
$$\cos\left(\theta_1-\theta_2\right) = \cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2 = c\cdot c + s\cdot s = c^2+s^2 .$$
Since $\theta_1$ realises $(c,s)$, we have $c^2+s^2 = \cos^2\theta_1 + \sin^2\theta_1 = 1$. Hence $\cos\left(\theta_1-\theta_2\right) = 1$, so by (T3)
$$\theta_1 - \theta_2 = 2k\pi \quad\text{for some } k \in \Z .$$
Now $\theta_1 \le \pi$ and $\theta_2 > -\pi$ give $\theta_1 - \theta_2 < 2\pi$; symmetrically $\theta_1 > -\pi$ and $\theta_2 \le \pi$ give $\theta_1-\theta_2 > -2\pi$. So $\left\lvert 2k\pi\right\rvert < 2\pi$, whence $\left\lvert k\right\rvert < 1$, so $k=0$ and $\theta_1 = \theta_2$. $\blacksquare$

**Consequence (proof strategy).** By Lemma 0 and Lemma 1, for each nonzero $\mathbf a$ it suffices to exhibit one angle $\theta_0$ such that

1. $\theta_0 \in (-\pi,\pi]$, and
2. $r\cos\theta_0 = x$ and $r\sin\theta_0 = y$;

then $\theta_0$ is a direction of $\mathbf a$, it lies in the prescribed interval, and it is the only such angle, so $\theta = \theta_0$. Since the six cases below are exhaustive, this also proves that every nonzero $\mathbf a$ *has* a direction in $(-\pi,\pi]$.

### Lemma 2 (the computational lemma)

**Lemma 2.** Let $x \ne 0$ and $y \in \R$; put $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $\phi := \arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right)$. Then $r > 0$ and
$$\cos\phi = \frac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{r}, \qquad \sin\phi = \frac{y\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{r\,x} .$$
Explicitly: if $x>0$ then $\cos\phi = \dfrac xr$ and $\sin\phi = \dfrac yr$; if $x<0$ then $\cos\phi = -\dfrac xr$ and $\sin\phi = -\dfrac yr$.

*Proof.* Since $x \ne 0$, the quotient $\dfrac yx$ is defined, and $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \ge \sqrt{x^2} = \left\lvert x\right\rvert > 0$.

By (A1), $\phi \in \openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ and $\tan\phi = \dfrac yx$. As $\cos\phi > 0$ on that interval, (T1) applies and gives
$$\frac1{\cos^2\phi} = 1 + \tan^2\phi = 1 + \frac{y^2}{x^2} = \frac{x^2+y^2}{x^2} = \frac{r^2}{x^2},$$
so that
$$\cos^2\phi = \frac{x^2}{r^2}, \qquad \left\lvert\cos\phi\right\rvert = \frac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{r}.$$
Both $\cos\phi$ and $\dfrac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{r}$ are strictly positive, so the absolute values may be dropped:
$$\cos\phi = \frac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{r}.$$
Since $\cos\phi \ne 0$, (T1) gives $\sin\phi = \tan\phi\cos\phi$, i.e.
$$\sin\phi = \frac yx\cdot\frac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{r} = \frac{y\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{r\,x} .$$
The explicit forms follow on substituting $\left\lvert x\right\rvert = x$ (for $x>0$) and $\left\lvert x\right\rvert = -x$ (for $x<0$). $\blacksquare$

---

## Part III. The six cases

Throughout, $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.

### III.1 Case $x>0$

Here $r \ge \left\lvert x\right\rvert > 0$, so $\mathbf a \ne \mathbf 0$ and it has a well-defined direction. Put
$$\theta_0 := \arctan\left(\frac yx\right).$$

*Range.* By (A1), $\theta_0 \in \openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2} \subset (-\pi,\pi]$.

*Components.* By Lemma 2 (case $x>0$),
$$\cos\theta_0 = \frac xr, \qquad \sin\theta_0 = \frac yr,$$
so $r\cos\theta_0 = x$ and $r\sin\theta_0 = y$.

By the Consequence of Lemma 1, $\theta = \theta_0 = \arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right)$.

### III.2 Case $x<0$, $y \ge 0$

Again $r \ge \left\lvert x\right\rvert > 0$. Put
$$\phi := \arctan\left(\frac yx\right), \qquad \theta_0 := \phi + \pi .$$

*Range.* Since $x<0$ and $y \ge 0$, we have $\dfrac yx \le 0$; by (A2), $\phi \in \left(-\dfrac\pi2,\ 0\right]$. Hence
$$\theta_0 = \phi + \pi \in \left(\frac\pi2,\ \pi\right] \subset (-\pi,\pi] .$$
(The upper endpoint $\pi$ is attained exactly when $y=0$, and it belongs to $(-\pi,\pi]$ because that interval is closed on the right.)

*Components.* By Lemma 2 (case $x<0$), $\cos\phi = -\dfrac xr$ and $\sin\phi = -\dfrac yr$. So by (T2),
$$\cos\theta_0 = \cos(\phi+\pi) = -\cos\phi = \frac xr, \qquad
\sin\theta_0 = \sin(\phi+\pi) = -\sin\phi = \frac yr,$$
whence $r\cos\theta_0 = x$ and $r\sin\theta_0 = y$.

By the Consequence of Lemma 1, $\theta = \theta_0 = \arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) + \pi$.

### III.3 Case $x<0$, $y<0$

Again $r \ge \left\lvert x\right\rvert > 0$. Put
$$\phi := \arctan\left(\frac yx\right), \qquad \theta_0 := \phi - \pi .$$

*Range.* Since $x<0$ and $y<0$, we have $\dfrac yx > 0$; by (A2), $\phi \in \left(0,\ \dfrac\pi2\right)$. Hence
$$\theta_0 = \phi - \pi \in \left(-\pi,\ -\frac\pi2\right) \subset (-\pi,\pi] .$$
(Crucially $\phi > 0$ *strictly*, so $\theta_0 > -\pi$ strictly and the excluded endpoint $-\pi$ is never attained.)

*Components.* By Lemma 2 (case $x<0$), $\cos\phi = -\dfrac xr$ and $\sin\phi = -\dfrac yr$. So by (T2),
$$\cos\theta_0 = \cos(\phi-\pi) = -\cos\phi = \frac xr, \qquad
\sin\theta_0 = \sin(\phi-\pi) = -\sin\phi = \frac yr,$$
whence $r\cos\theta_0 = x$ and $r\sin\theta_0 = y$.

By the Consequence of Lemma 1, $\theta = \theta_0 = \arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) - \pi$.

### III.4 Case $x=0$, $y>0$

Here $r = \sqrt{0+y^2} = \left\lvert y\right\rvert = y > 0$, so $\mathbf a \ne \mathbf 0$. Put $\theta_0 := \dfrac\pi2 \in (-\pi,\pi]$. Since $\cos\dfrac\pi2 = 0$ and $\sin\dfrac\pi2 = 1$,
$$r\cos\theta_0 = y\cdot 0 = 0 = x, \qquad r\sin\theta_0 = y\cdot1 = y .$$
By the Consequence of Lemma 1, $\theta = \dfrac\pi2$.

### III.5 Case $x=0$, $y<0$

Here $r = \left\lvert y\right\rvert = -y > 0$, so $\mathbf a \ne \mathbf 0$. Put $\theta_0 := -\dfrac\pi2 \in (-\pi,\pi]$. Since $\cos\left(-\dfrac\pi2\right) = 0$ and $\sin\left(-\dfrac\pi2\right) = -1$,
$$r\cos\theta_0 = (-y)\cdot0 = 0 = x, \qquad r\sin\theta_0 = (-y)\cdot(-1) = y .$$
By the Consequence of Lemma 1, $\theta = -\dfrac\pi2$.

### III.6 Case $x=0$, $y=0$

Then $\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$, and by §I.3 its direction is undefined.

---

## Part IV. Conclusion

The six cases
$$x>0; \quad x<0,\,y\ge0; \quad x<0,\,y<0; \quad x=0,\,y>0; \quad x=0,\,y<0; \quad x=0,\,y=0$$
are mutually exclusive and together exhaust $\R^2$: indeed, either $x>0$, or $x<0$ (split according to $y\ge0$ or $y<0$), or $x=0$ (split according to $y>0$, $y<0$ or $y=0$).

In each of the five cases with $\mathbf a \ne \mathbf 0$ we produced an angle $\theta_0$ lying in $(-\pi,\pi]$ and satisfying the characterisation $(\ast)$ of Lemma 0; by Lemma 1 that angle is unique in $(-\pi,\pi]$, hence equals the direction $\theta$ of $\mathbf a$. In the remaining case $\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$ the direction is undefined. This is exactly the asserted case formula:
$$\theta = \begin{cases}
\arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) & x > 0\\[2pt]
\arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) + \pi & x < 0,\ y \ge 0\\[2pt]
\arctan\left(\dfrac yx\right) - \pi & x < 0,\ y < 0\\[2pt]
\dfrac\pi2 & x = 0,\ y > 0\\[2pt]
-\dfrac\pi2 & x = 0,\ y < 0\\[2pt]
\text{undefined} & x = 0,\ y = 0 .
\end{cases}$$
$\blacksquare$

---

## Remark (consistency checks)

* The three $\arctan$ branches cover the three "signs" of $x$-half-plane data and produce, respectively, values in $\left(-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right)$ (right half-plane), $\left(\dfrac\pi2,\pi\right]$ (second quadrant together with the negative $x$-axis) and $\left(-\pi,-\dfrac\pi2\right)$ (third quadrant); together with $\pm\dfrac\pi2$ these are pairwise disjoint subsets of $(-\pi,\pi]$, as must be the case since distinct directions correspond to distinct rays.
* The negative $x$-axis ($x<0$, $y=0$) receives $\theta = \pi$ and not $\theta = -\pi$, consistent with the convention that the interval is half-open on the left; this is why $y=0$ is grouped with $y>0$ in the second branch.
* Along the positive $x$-axis ($x>0$, $y=0$) the formula gives $\theta = \arctan 0 = 0$, as it must.
